title: Jewish life in Jesus's day
seoTitle: Jewish Life in Jesus's Day: What It Was Really Like
description: A long, sourced portrait of the world Jesus lived in: the land and its rulers, a day and a year, the Temple, the synagogue, the groups, the hopes, and family, sickness and death.
line: Galilee and Judea in the first century: what people saw, ate, paid, feared and hoped, with the evidence named as we go.
intro: This is a portrait of the world Jesus grew up in: the villages of Galilee and the city of Jerusalem in the first century, in the years before the Romans burned the Temple in AD 70. It does not argue one point. It tries to show what people saw, ate, paid, feared and hoped, so that the Gospels read like reports from a real place, because they are.

Each part names its evidence as it goes. Most of it comes from three kinds of witness. There is Josephus, a Jewish priest and general who wrote his histories in Rome between the 70s and the 90s AD. There are the Dead Sea Scrolls and other Jewish writings from before and around Jesus's time. And there is the spade: boats, tombs, coins, stone cups and inscriptions. Much of what is often said about this world comes from the Mishnah, a collection of rabbinic rulings written down around AD 200. Where this portrait uses it, it says so, because a rule recorded 170 years after Jesus may or may not describe the world he knew. Where historians disagree, or the evidence is thin, it says that too.

One more thing before the first part. Jesus, his family and all his first followers were Jews inside this world. The Pharisees, the priests and the crowds in these pages are described as their own best sources describe them, not as later Christian sermons often did.

parts.title: The land and who ruled it
parts.line: A small country, walked on foot, under a king's sons and a Roman prefect.
body: The whole country was small enough to walk, and nearly everyone did walk it. Josephus, who commanded the Jewish forces in Galilee when the war with Rome began in AD 66, says that a traveler in a hurry could go from Galilee to Jerusalem in three days by cutting straight through Samaria (Life 269). The other road ran down the Jordan valley and climbed to Jerusalem from Jericho, out of the hot country below sea level. That is why the Gospels always have people going up to Jerusalem and down to Jericho.

Four regions matter most in the Gospels. Galilee, in the north, was green and crowded farm country around a freshwater lake about 21 kilometers long and 13 wide, which the Gospels call the Sea of Galilee, the lake of Gennesaret and the Sea of Tiberias. Josephus praises its rich soil and says the villages were so full of people that the smallest held more than fifteen thousand (Jewish War 3.43). No historian takes that number at face value, but the picture of a crowded countryside rings true. Judea, in the south, was drier hill country with Jerusalem at its heart. Between the two lay Samaria. East and south of the lake lay the Decapolis, a league of Greek cities. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder lists ten of them, from Damascus in the north to Philadelphia (modern Amman) in the south, and admits that not everyone agreed on the list (Natural History 5.74). Only one, Scythopolis, lay west of the Jordan. In those cities people kept pigs, spoke Greek and worshiped Greek gods. A Galilean fisherman who rowed to the far shore crossed into another way of life.

Who ruled you depended on where you stood. Herod the Great was king over the whole land from 37 BC until his death, which most historians date to 4 BC. A minority argue for 1 BC, and the question turns on which eclipse of the moon Josephus meant when he said one came shortly before Herod died. Rome divided Herod's kingdom among three of his sons. Archelaus took Judea, Samaria and Idumea, ruled them so harshly that Augustus removed him in AD 6, and from then on Judea had a Roman governor. Herod Antipas took Galilee and Perea, the land across the Jordan, and held them until AD 39. Josephus says those two regions paid him two hundred talents a year (Antiquities 17.318). Philip took the lands north and east of the lake. So when Jesus walked from Nazareth to Jerusalem, he left the land of a Jewish prince who answered to Rome and entered a Roman province.

The Roman governor of Judea held the title prefect and lived on the coast at Caesarea, the harbor city Herod had built in the Roman style. In 1961 Italian archaeologists digging in its theater found a stone, reused as a step, that names "Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea" and a building he dedicated to the emperor Tiberius. It is the only ancient inscription known that names him. Pilate governed from about AD 26 to 36 and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts, when the crowds were largest and trouble most likely. In Jerusalem the high priest Caiaphas held office from about AD 18 to 36. In 1990 builders in Jerusalem's Peace Forest broke into a family tomb that held an ornate bone box inscribed in Aramaic, usually read "Joseph son of Caiaphas." Many scholars think it held the high priest's bones. Some are not sure.

Direct Roman rule in Judea began with a count of people and property for tax under Quirinius, the governor of Syria, in AD 6. Josephus says a man named Judas rose against it, teaching that the tax was the first step into slavery and that God alone was Israel's ruler and lord (Antiquities 18.4; 18.23). Acts remembers him as Judas the Galilean, who "perished" (Acts 5:37). The revolt failed. The question it asked did not go away. A generation later it was put to Jesus in the Temple courts, with a Roman coin in his hand.

Most people lived in villages. Nazareth sat on a ridge above the Jezreel valley. Recent estimates put its people at a few hundred, often given as 200 to 500. The evidence is thin, and those numbers are careful guesses. Its houses were small and built of fieldstone, with cisterns, storage pits and caves cut into the soft rock. About five or six kilometers to the north, an hour or so on foot, stood Sepphoris. The Roman general Varus burned it in the unrest after Herod's death, and Antipas rebuilt it as his capital (Antiquities 17.289; 18.27). Later Antipas built a new capital on the lake and named it Tiberias after the emperor. Josephus says the site held old graves, so that Jews who settled there were ritually unclean under the law, and Antipas had to give people houses and land to make them stay (Antiquities 18.36-38). The Gospels never mention Sepphoris at all, and they name Tiberias only in passing (John 6:23).

Time ran on a different clock. A day began at sunset and ran to the next sunset, as the days of Genesis 1 run from evening to morning. The hours of daylight were counted from sunrise, so "the third hour" in Mark 15:25 is mid-morning and "the ninth hour" is mid-afternoon. Months followed the moon. The year of feasts began in spring, in the month of Nisan, and the Passover lamb was killed on the fourteenth day of that month and eaten that night (Exodus 12:6-8; Leviticus 23:5-6). Years were not numbered from one starting point but dated by rulers, which is why Luke dates John the Baptist to the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius (Luke 3:1).

read.text: At that very hour, some Pharisees came to Jesus and told Him, “Leave this place and get away, because Herod wants to kill You.” But Jesus replied, “Go tell that fox, ‘Look, I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow, and on the third day I will reach My goal.’
read.note: Galilee belonged to Herod Antipas, the man who had already beheaded John the Baptist. Jesus is inside his territory when he calls him a fox, a small and cunning animal, not a lion. Notice too who brings the warning: Pharisees, trying to keep him alive.

read.text: “You are a Jew,” said the woman. “How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.)
read.note: Samaritans worshiped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses, but at their own mountain, Gerizim. Coins and other finds show that the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple there around 111 or 110 BC. Josephus tells of Samaritans who slipped into the Temple at Passover and scattered human bones to defile it (Antiquities 18.29-30), and of Galilean pilgrims killed at the village of Ginea on their way through Samaria (Antiquities 20.118). The old wound is under the woman's words.

read.text: There on the nearby hillside a large herd of pigs was feeding. So the demons begged Jesus, “Send us to the pigs, so that we may enter them.” He gave them permission, and the unclean spirits came out and went into the pigs, and the herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the water.
read.note: This happens on the eastern shore, in the country of the Greek cities. A herd of two thousand pigs tells a Jewish listener at once that this is gentile land. Jesus has crossed the lake into a foreign world, and a man that world had chained among the tombs is the one he came for.

parts.title: A day and a year
parts.line: The house, the bread, the work, the debts, the Sabbath and the road up to the feasts.
body: A family lived close together. Excavated houses in Galilean towns such as Capernaum are clusters of small rooms around an open courtyard, where related households shared an oven, a hand mill and a cistern. Walls were built of whatever stone lay nearest, black basalt around the lake. Roofs were wooden beams covered with branches and packed earth, flat enough to sleep on in summer and soft enough to dig through. That is what four friends did in Capernaum when the crowd at the door was too thick (Mark 2:4).

The scholar Kenneth Bailey, who spent decades in the villages of the Middle East, argued that many such houses kept the family's animals at one end of the main room at night, with a guest room built on or above. On his reading, the "inn" of Luke 2:7 is that guest room, already full, and the baby was laid in a feeding trough inside a family home rather than in a stable. Not everyone accepts this. But the word Luke uses there, kataluma, is the same word he uses for the upper room where Jesus ate the Last Supper (Luke 22:11), and it is not his word for a commercial inn (Luke 10:34).

Bread was the meal. Historians of the ancient diet reckon that bread made up at least half of what ordinary people ate, and perhaps much more (Susan Weingarten, drawing on the work of Magen Broshi). The grain was ground each morning on a hand mill, a heavy daily job that the Gospels take for granted when they speak of two women grinding together (Matthew 24:41). With the bread came olive oil, lentils and beans, olives, figs, dates, onions, cheese and wine. Fish from the lake was eaten fresh near the shore and salted or dried farther away. Meat was for a feast: a wedding, an honored guest, a sacrifice. When Jesus taught his followers to ask for their daily bread, he named the thing most of them worried about every day.

Most people farmed, and most farmers had little to spare. Grain, wine and oil were the three great crops, as they had been since Deuteronomy. Around the lake men fished with nets from wooden boats. In 1986, when a drought lowered the water, two men from Kibbutz Ginosar spotted the outline of one in the mud. It is about 8.2 meters long and 2.3 meters wide, and carbon tests, pottery and coins found with it date it to between the first century BC and the first century AD. It is the kind of boat the Gospels have in mind. Others worked as builders and craftsmen, the trade the Gospels give to Joseph and to Jesus (Mark 6:3), in a land where Herod and his sons were building whole cities.

Below the farmers who owned a little land were the day laborers, hired in the marketplace in the morning and paid at sunset, like the men in Jesus's story of the vineyard (Matthew 20:1-16). Below them were people in debt. Debt runs all through the Gospels: in the Lord's Prayer, in parables about loans forgiven, and in the servant whose master orders him sold with his wife and children to pay what he owed (Matthew 18:25). This was not only a picture. When the war against Rome broke out in AD 66, Josephus says, the rebels in Jerusalem set fire to the public archives to destroy the moneylenders' bonds and win the debtors to their side (Jewish War 2.427).

A Galilean paid several masters. Antipas took his taxes on land and produce. Tolls were charged on goods moving along the roads and across borders, collected by men who bid for the right to collect them; the Gospels call them tax collectors, and Levi sat at one such booth beside the lake at Capernaum (Mark 2:1, 13-14). In Judea after AD 6 the tribute went to Rome itself. On top of this came the dues the law of Moses required: tithes of produce for the priests and Levites, and the half-shekel for the Temple. Money came in three kinds at once. There was Roman silver, like the denarius with the emperor's head that Jesus asked to be shown; Greek silver, like the drachma; and small local bronze coins. Herod and Antipas struck their bronze coins without human faces, out of respect for the commandment against images.

Every seventh day the work stopped. To outsiders this was the strangest Jewish custom of all. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing about AD 100, sneered that the Jews had given the seventh day over to idleness (Histories 5.4). To Jews it was a gift and a sign of the covenant, and some kept it at great cost. When the Maccabees rose against the Greek king Antiochus in the 160s BC, about a thousand faithful Jews let themselves be killed rather than fight on the Sabbath, until Mattathias and his friends decided that they would defend themselves on that day (1 Maccabees 2:29-41). By Jesus's time Jews disagreed about what counted as work. The Damascus Document, a rule found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, forbids helping an animal give birth on the Sabbath and says that if it falls into a pit, no one is to lift it out until the day is over (CD 11.13-14). Other Jews were not so strict, and Jesus could count on that.

Three times a year the law called every Israelite man to appear before the Lord (Deuteronomy 16:16): at Passover in spring, at the Feast of Weeks fifty days later (Pentecost, in Greek), and at the Feast of Booths in autumn after the harvest. Not everyone went every time, but many did, and whole villages traveled together. That is how Mary and Joseph could walk a full day before they noticed their twelve-year-old was missing (Luke 2:44). Josephus says that a Roman governor once had the priests count the Passover lambs to measure the crowd, and the count came to 256,500 (Jewish War 6.422-425). From that he reckoned the pilgrims in the millions, which historians think far too high. Joachim Jeremias estimated about 125,000 visitors at Passover besides the city's own people, and that too is a careful guess. Either way, for a week the city overflowed: pilgrims camped on the hills around it, houses took in strangers, and the roads up were crowded. Fifteen of the Psalms (120 to 134) each open with the words "A song of ascents," and many readers think they were sung on the way up.

read.text: Then a paralytic was brought to Him, carried by four men. Since they were unable to get to Jesus through the crowd, they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening, and lowered the paralytic on his mat.
read.note: A packed-earth roof over wooden beams could be opened and patched again the next day. The four men are not vandals. They are doing something any villager could picture, and the crowd was too thick at the door because the whole house opened onto one small courtyard.

read.text: “For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. He agreed to pay them a denarius for the day and sent them into his vineyard.
read.note: A denarius was a fair wage for a day's work in the fields, and a day laborer had nothing put by. A man hired at the eleventh hour, near five in the afternoon, expected to take home almost nothing, and his family would eat less that night. The landowner's generosity is felt at the supper table.

read.text: He replied, “If one of you has a sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will he not take hold of it and lift it out?
read.note: The strictest Jews of the day, the community of the Damascus Document, said you must not lift the animal out. Jesus assumes the Galileans in front of him would lift it out without a second thought. He is not arguing against Judaism. He is arguing inside it, from what his hearers already do.

parts.title: The Temple
parts.line: What a pilgrim saw, heard and smelled, who served there, who paid for it, and the fire that ended it.
body: First-century Jerusalem was a temple with a city around it. Herod began rebuilding the Temple in the eighteenth year of his reign, about 20 or 19 BC (Antiquities 15.380). The sanctuary itself went up within a few years, but work on the courts and porches went on for decades, which is why the crowd in John's Gospel says the building has taken forty-six years. To hold it all, Herod built a vast level platform out over the slopes of the hill, walled with dressed stone. One block in the western wall, now visible in the tunnel that runs beside it, is about 13.6 meters long. Estimates of its weight range from about 250 tons to well over 500. When a disciple said, "Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!" (Mark 13:1), he said what every pilgrim said.

A pilgrim came up from the south and climbed through the gates into the great outer court. Anyone could enter it, Jew or gentile. Long covered porches ran around its edges, and the Gospels place Jesus teaching in one of them, Solomon's Colonnade (John 10:23). Here too the business of the Temple went on, and it was business the law required. Pilgrims who had walked for days could not drive a lamb from Galilee or carry doves from Alexandria, so animals and birds were sold near the altar that needed them, and coins from a dozen mints had to be changed into the one coin the Temple accepted.

Farther in, a low barrier marked how far a non-Jew could go. Stone notices set along it, in Greek and in Latin, warned foreigners not to pass, on pain of death. Josephus describes them (Jewish War 5.193-194). In 1871 the French scholar Charles Clermont-Ganneau found one complete, its Greek wording very close to what Josephus says, and a broken second copy came to light in 1936. Historians still argue over whether anyone was ever actually put to death under it. Past the barrier, steps led up to the inner courts: a court where Jewish women and men could go, then a court for Jewish men, then the priests' court with the great altar, and at the center the sanctuary. Its innermost room, the Holy of Holies, was entered once a year, by the high priest alone, on the Day of Atonement.

It was loud, and it smelled. At the great feasts thousands of animals were brought in and killed, and their blood was splashed at the altar and drained away. The smoke of burning fat rose all day. Incense was burned in the sanctuary every morning and every evening (Exodus 30:7-8). Levites sang psalms, and trumpets sounded.

It is easy to think of sacrifice as a way of buying off an angry God. E. P. Sanders, in his study of the religion as it was practiced (Judaism: Practice and Belief, 1992), showed how badly that picture fits the sources. There were offerings of thanks and offerings shared as a family feast, as well as offerings for sin and cleansing, and all of them were understood as the way God himself had given his people to come near him. The poor were provided for. A family that could not afford a lamb could bring two doves or two young pigeons (Leviticus 12:8), which is exactly what Mary and Joseph brought after Jesus was born (Luke 2:24).

The priesthood passed from father to son. Following 1 Chronicles 24, the priests were divided into twenty-four divisions that took turns serving, and within a division the tasks were assigned by lot. Luke's first scene is a country priest, Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, chosen by lot to burn the incense (Luke 1:8-9). Above the ordinary priests stood a few powerful families, the chief priests, who ran the Temple and the city's leading council. Herod, and later the Romans, appointed high priests and removed them as it suited them. That is the house of Annas and Caiaphas, and it lived by keeping the peace with Rome.

Every Jewish man paid half a shekel a year for the Temple, a duty drawn from Exodus 30:13, and Jews sent it to Jerusalem from all over the Roman world. The coin used was the shekel of Tyre, a Phoenician city on the coast. It was very nearly pure silver, purer than Roman coins, and it carried the head of Tyre's god Melqart, whom Greeks called Herakles, on one side and an eagle on the other. The purity of the silver seems to have counted for more than the pagan image. One such coin paid the half-shekel for two men, which is the coin Peter finds in the fish (Matthew 17:27). The money changers whose tables Jesus overturned were turning pilgrims' money into these.

In the summer of AD 70, at the end of a long siege, Roman soldiers under Titus burned the Temple. Josephus, who watched from the Roman side, says it fell on the tenth day of the month of Lous (Av), the same day of the year on which the king of Babylon had burned the first Temple (Jewish War 6.250). Afterward the emperor Vespasian ordered every Jew, wherever he lived, to pay the same two drachmas each year to the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol in Rome (Jewish War 7.218). The tax Jesus had paid for himself and Peter now paid for a pagan god. With the Temple gone, the sacrifices stopped, the priests lost their work, and the Sadducees soon vanish from history. Jewish teachers rebuilt the life of the people around the study of the law, prayer and the synagogue, and the first Christians read Jesus's words about the Temple in the light of that fire.

read.text: Jesus answered, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.” “This temple took forty-six years to build,” the Jews replied, “and You are going to raise it up in three days?”
read.note: The Temple was still a building site when Jesus spoke. To the crowd, forty-six years of Herod's work stood behind their reply, and the stones were real. John tells his readers, who knew the Temple had since burned, that Jesus had been speaking about his own body.

read.text: When they arrived in Jerusalem, Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. And He would not allow anyone to carry merchandise through the temple courts. Then Jesus began to teach them, and He declared, “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’”
read.note: The money changers and dove sellers were not a scandal everyone else had missed. Their trade made the sacrifices the law required possible. Jesus quotes Isaiah 56, a house of prayer for all the nations, in the one court where the nations were allowed to stand, and Jeremiah 7, spoken against a Temple that was later destroyed. The chief priests heard a threat to the whole arrangement.

read.text: After they had arrived in Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax came to Peter and asked, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” “Yes,” he answered. When Peter entered the house, Jesus preempted him. “What do you think, Simon?” He asked. “From whom do the kings of the earth collect customs and taxes: from their own sons, or from others?” “From others,” Peter answered. “Then the sons are exempt,” Jesus declared. “But so that we may not offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish you catch. When you open its mouth, you will find a four-drachma coin. Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.”
read.note: The four-drachma coin was the Tyrian shekel, enough to pay the half-shekel for two. Jesus says the king's sons are free, and pays anyway, so as not to give offense. Matthew's first readers, after AD 70, were paying those same two drachmas to Jupiter in Rome.

parts.title: Synagogue, Scripture and school
parts.line: Where the law was read and taught each week, in which languages, and who could read it.
body: If the Temple held the year, the synagogue held the week. The word is Greek and means a gathering. Before AD 70 it could mean the community that met as much as the room it met in, and some gatherings met in a large house or an open place rather than a building of their own (Lee Levine, The Ancient Synagogue, 2000). What they did there is not in doubt. Philo, the Jewish philosopher of Alexandria who was writing in Jesus's lifetime, says that on every seventh day thousands of schools stood open in every city, teaching good sense, self-control, courage and justice (Special Laws 2.62). Josephus says Moses ordered the people to leave their other work every week and gather to hear the law and learn it thoroughly, something no other lawgiver had thought to do (Against Apion 2.175).

Archaeologists have now found several meeting halls from before 70: at Gamla in the Golan, at Herod's fortresses of Masada and Herodium, and since 2009 at Magdala on the shore of the lake, the home town of Mary Magdalene. The Magdala hall had stone benches along its walls, so that the gathering faced the middle of the room, and a carved stone block that shows a seven-branched lampstand, one of the oldest carvings of the Temple menorah known. In Jerusalem itself, an inscription in Greek found in the early twentieth century records that a priest and leader of a synagogue named Theodotus built his synagogue "for the reading of the law and for the teaching of the commandments," with a guest house, rooms and water installations for visitors from abroad. Most scholars date it before 70. It describes a room very like the one at Nazareth in Luke 4.

A Sabbath gathering centered on reading. Someone read from the law of Moses, and often a passage from the prophets after it, and then someone sat down to explain it, which is what Jesus does at Nazareth (Luke 4:20). Prayer surrounded the reading. Josephus says Moses commanded the people to recall before God, twice each day, at the start of the day and at bedtime, what he had done in bringing them out of Egypt (Antiquities 4.212). Many scholars think he is describing the Shema, the confession of Deuteronomy 6:4-9 that begins "Hear, O Israel." Others warn that the set prayers known from the later rabbis may have taken their fixed form after 70. Small leather boxes for the words of the law, worn on the arm and forehead as Deuteronomy 6:8 commands, have been found in the caves at Qumran.

People in Galilee spoke three languages, unevenly. At home and in the market they spoke Aramaic, the language of the street since the exile. The Gospels keep some of Jesus's own words in it: "Talitha koum" to a dead girl, "Ephphatha" to a deaf man, and from the cross, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" (Mark 5:41; 7:34; 15:34). Hebrew was the language of Scripture and prayer, and most of the Dead Sea Scrolls are written in it. Greek was the language of trade, government and the cities. The papers of a Jewish woman named Babatha, hidden in a cave near the Dead Sea during the revolt that began in AD 132, show all of this in one bundle: contracts written in Greek, signed by witnesses in Aramaic or in the Aramaic of the Nabataeans. The notice over Jesus's cross was written in three languages for the same reason (John 19:20).

How many people could read? Probably very few, though historians argue about how few. Meir Bar-Ilan estimated that only about three percent of Jews in the land could read, and Catherine Hezser's large study of Jewish literacy in Roman Palestine (2001) concluded that writing was mostly in the hands of the political, priestly and wealthy classes. Others think that many more could read a little without being able to write. A book was a costly object. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied in the late second century BC, is about 7.3 meters long and holds 54 columns, for one book of the Bible. A village might own a few scrolls, kept for the gathering, and not much more.

So most people knew Scripture the way they knew songs, by hearing it, saying it and remembering it. A scribe was a man with the time and training to read, write and explain the law. Writing in the early second century BC, Ben Sira said it plainly: "The wisdom of the scribe depends on the opportunity of leisure" (Sirach 38:24, RSV), and he goes on to list the farmer, the smith and the potter, who keep the world running but have no time for study. Against that background the question in John 7:15, how this man has such learning without having studied, is the question of people who knew where Jesus came from.

read.text: Then Jesus came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up. As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath. And when He stood up to read, the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Him. Unrolling it, He found the place where it was written:
read.note: This is a village gathering of a few hundred people at most, with one scroll handed over by the attendant. The reader stood out of respect for the text and sat down to teach. Jesus does both in the room he had sat in as a boy, in front of people who knew his family.

read.text: Now one of the scribes had come up and heard their debate. Noticing how well Jesus had answered them, he asked Him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” Jesus replied, “This is the most important: ‘Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’
read.note: Jesus answers with the Shema, the words every Jewish child heard, and then joins it to Leviticus 19:18 on loving your neighbor. The scribe who asked was not an opponent. He agreed, and Jesus told him he was not far from the kingdom of God (Mark 12:32-34).

read.text: Taking her by the hand, Jesus said, “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!”
read.note: Mark writes in Greek for readers who did not know Aramaic, so he keeps the two words and translates them. It is one of the few places in the Gospels where you hear the sound of Jesus's own voice, speaking to a child in the language of her home.

parts.title: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and the rest
parts.line: The parties of the day as their own best sources describe them, and the people outside them.
body: Josephus tells his Greek and Roman readers that the Jews had three schools of thought, the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Essenes, and a fourth that grew up in his own century (Antiquities 18.11-25). He describes them as philosophies because his readers knew what a philosophy was. It is worth remembering what he does not say: most Jews belonged to none of them. Farmers, fishermen and their families went to the gathering on the Sabbath, went up to the feasts, kept the law as their parents had, and looked to these groups for teaching and argument without joining one.

The Pharisees were the most popular. Josephus says they handed on to the people many practices received from their fathers that are not written in the law of Moses, and that the Sadducees rejected these (Antiquities 13.297). They believed in the resurrection of the dead, and in God's providence alongside real human choice. Josephus says they had such influence with ordinary people that even Sadducees in office went along with their teaching, though he may be flattering a group he himself followed (Antiquities 18.15, 17). They were not many. Josephus counts more than six thousand who refused to swear loyalty to Caesar and to Herod (Antiquities 17.42). Most were not priests but lay people who tried to keep the law's rules of tithing and purity in ordinary life, and how far they went in that is still argued between scholars such as Jacob Neusner and E. P. Sanders.

They argued with Jesus because they were close to him. They cared about the same questions: the Sabbath, purity, divorce, how to keep the law with the whole heart. Some warned him that Antipas wanted him dead (Luke 13:31). Nicodemus was one of them. So was Gamaliel, "honored by all the people," who told the council to leave the apostles alone (Acts 5:34), and so was Paul (Philippians 3:5). In later Christian speech "Pharisee" came to mean a hypocrite. That was not what the word meant to Jesus's hearers. When he says, as he does in Matthew 23, that some of them do not practice what they teach, he is making an argument inside a family about its own best people.

The Sadducees were few and powerful. They were drawn from the priestly and wealthy families around the Temple. They held only to the written law, rejected the Pharisees' traditions, and said there is no resurrection, no angels and no spirits (Acts 23:8). Josephus says their teaching reached only a few, but those few were men of the highest rank (Antiquities 18.17). Their power rested on the Temple, and when the Temple fell in AD 70 they disappear from the record.

The Essenes kept apart. Philo and Josephus both put their number at about four thousand (Every Good Man Is Free 75; Antiquities 18.20). They shared their goods, ate in common and kept the Sabbath with great strictness. The Roman writer Pliny describes a community of them on the western shore of the Dead Sea, living without women and without money, with only palm trees for company (Natural History 5.73). Between 1947 and 1956 the remains of about 900 scrolls were found in eleven caves near the ruins of Qumran, on that same shore. Most scholars connect the people who kept them with the Essenes or a branch of them, though not all agree. The scrolls include copies of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, and the group's own rules and hymns. Their Community Rule calls its members the sons of light and speaks of keeping its rules "until the coming of a prophet and the messiahs of Aaron and Israel" (1QS 9.11), which most read as a priestly anointed one and a royal one. They believed the Temple's priests had gone wrong, and they withdrew to wait for God to set things right.

Then there were those who would not wait. Josephus says the fourth school, begun by Judas in AD 6, agreed with the Pharisees in most things but had a passion for liberty that could not be broken, held that God alone was their ruler and lord, and would call no man master (Antiquities 18.23). In the decades that followed, Josephus records men who led crowds into the desert promising signs from God, such as Theudas (Antiquities 20.97-98; Acts 5:36), and the Romans killed them. The Zealots as a named party belong to the war of 66 to 70. When Luke calls one of the Twelve "Simon called the Zealot," he may mean a man of fierce zeal for the law rather than a member of a party that may not yet have existed.

Outside all the parties stood the people the Gospels call tax collectors and sinners. Toll collectors worked under contract for Antipas or for Rome and could take more than the rate, which is why John the Baptist told them, "Collect no more than you are authorized" (Luke 3:13). Zacchaeus at Jericho, a chief tax collector, was very wealthy (Luke 19:2). E. P. Sanders argued in Jesus and Judaism (1985) that "sinners" did not mean ordinary working people who were lax about purity. It meant the wicked, people who had put themselves outside the covenant by the way they lived. On that reading, what scandalized Jesus's critics was not that he talked to common folk but that he welcomed such people to his table before they had made the usual amends. Not every scholar accepts the whole of Sanders's case, but it has changed how the scenes are read.

read.text: “The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach.
read.note: Moses' seat was the place from which the law was taught. Jesus does not tell his hearers to ignore the Pharisees' teaching. He tells them to keep it, and to do better than some who teach it.

read.text: Then the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Jesus and questioned Him:
read.note: The Sadducees accepted only the written law, and they found no resurrection in it. Their riddle about a woman married to seven brothers was meant to make the idea look absurd. Jesus answers them from the books they did accept, from the burning bush in Exodus.

read.text: Matthew and Thomas; James son of Alphaeus and Simon called the Zealot;
read.note: In the same list sit Matthew, whom Matthew's Gospel calls the tax collector (Matthew 10:3), and Simon called the Zealot. One had collected money for the powers that ruled. The other's name speaks of zeal for God against them. Jesus called both.

parts.title: What people believed and hoped for
parts.line: One God, his people, his law, clean and unclean, and a kingdom many longed to see.
body: Beneath all the arguments lay a faith most Jews shared, which E. P. Sanders called common Judaism. There was one God, the maker of all things, who had chosen Israel and given it his law. Jews would not worship any other god or make images of their own, which made them odd in the eyes of their neighbors. In his study of the Jewish writings of the period (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977) Sanders argued that keeping the law was not understood as a way of earning God's favor. It was the grateful response of a people God had already chosen, and the sacrifices were there for when they failed.

Purity was part of that response, and it is often misread. Being unclean was not the same as being sinful or dirty. It was a state that came from ordinary life: childbirth, certain flows of blood, a skin disease, touching a dead body (Leviticus 12 to 15; Numbers 19). It mattered mainly because an unclean person could not enter the Temple until cleansed. Archaeologists have found stepped pools for washing by immersion in Jerusalem and across Judea and Galilee, and many cups, bowls and jars carved from soft white stone, because stone was held not to take on impurity the way pottery did. The rule is written down only in the Mishnah, around AD 200, but the stone vessels show the practice in Jesus's day. At Reina, near Nazareth and just south of the village many identify with Cana, archaeologists have dug out a cave workshop where such vessels were made. The find was announced in 2017.

The land and the Temple belonged to the same faith. God had given Israel the land, and he dwelt among them in his house. That is why foreign rule hurt so much. It was not only a matter of taxes. A gentile emperor's soldiers stood in the fortress beside God's house and his governor appointed God's high priest, and many asked how long God would allow it.

The answer many gave was the kingdom of God: the day God would rule openly, put things right, and gather his scattered people. How that would happen, and through whom, varied a great deal. The Psalms of Solomon, written after the Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, pray in their seventeenth psalm for a son of David to rise, to purge Jerusalem of the gentiles who had trampled it, and to rule in righteousness. The community of the scrolls looked for two anointed ones, a priest and a king. A small scroll fragment from Qumran known as 4Q521 says that the Lord will heal the wounded, give life to the dead and bring good news to the poor, words strikingly close to Jesus's answer to John the Baptist in Matthew 11. Many Jewish writings of the time mention no messiah at all. John J. Collins, in The Scepter and the Star (1995), shows how many different shapes the hope took. There was no single checklist the Messiah had to meet.

Many Jews also hoped for the resurrection of the dead. Daniel had spoken of those who sleep in the dust awaking (Daniel 12:2), and in 2 Maccabees a mother and her seven sons go to their deaths trusting that God would give them back their lives. The Pharisees taught it; the Sadducees denied it. Where it was believed, resurrection meant something that would happen to all God's people together at the end of the age, not to one man in the middle of history. N. T. Wright, in The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003), argued that this is part of what made the first Christians' claim about Jesus so startling to Jews who already believed in resurrection.

read.text: Now six stone water jars had been set there for the Jewish rites of purification. Each could hold from twenty to thirty gallons.
read.note: Six large stone jars at a village wedding tell you this family kept the purity customs carefully and could afford to. Stone vessel workshops have been found a short walk away. Jesus fills the jars that served the old washing with wine for the feast.

read.text: Meanwhile John heard in prison about the works of Christ, and he sent his disciples to ask Him, “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” Jesus replied, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.
read.note: John expected a judge with an axe and a fire. Jesus answers with a list drawn from Isaiah: the blind, the lame, the deaf, the dead, good news for the poor. A scroll from Qumran used almost the same list for what God would do in the last days. John would have understood the answer as a claim.

read.text: Martha replied, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.”
read.note: Martha already believes in the resurrection, as a Pharisee would, at the last day for everyone. Jesus answers that the resurrection is standing in front of her. That is the surprise the first Christians kept trying to explain.

parts.title: Family, honor, sickness and death
parts.line: Marriage and divorce, women and children, slaves, the sick, and how the dead were buried.
body: Life was lived in households, not as single people. Marriages were arranged between families, and betrothal was binding in a way an engagement is not today: to end it took a divorce. That is why Matthew calls Joseph Mary's husband before they lived together, and why his kindness was to divorce her quietly rather than in public (Matthew 1:19). Girls were probably married in their teens, though the evidence is scattered and comes from many places and periods.

Divorce was a man's right under the law of Deuteronomy 24, and Jews argued over its grounds. Josephus, setting out the law for his Roman readers, says a man who wished to divorce his wife could do so for any cause whatever (Antiquities 4.253), and that is almost word for word the question the Pharisees put to Jesus in Matthew 19:3. The Mishnah, compiled about AD 200, records the schools of Shammai and Hillel taking opposite sides on the same verse. Jesus answered by going behind Deuteronomy to Genesis, to what marriage was at the beginning.

Families lived by honor. A household's good name in the village was its wealth, and public shame could ruin it for a generation. Bruce Malina's The New Testament World (1981) set out how this shaped everything from a dinner invitation to an insult, and it explains a great deal in the parables: a son who demands his inheritance early, a father who runs down the road, a host whose guests all make excuses.

Women ran households, worked in the fields and the market, and could own property; Babatha's papers record her buying, lending and going to court. But the law was written for men. Josephus says that the testimony of women was not to be admitted, "because of the levity and boldness of their sex" (Antiquities 4.219, in Whiston's translation). The Gospels name women among those who traveled with Jesus and supported his work from their own means, among them Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager (Luke 8:1-3). And the Gospels make women the first witnesses of the empty tomb, the very witnesses a court would have set aside.

Children were many and died often. No exact figures exist for Galilee, but across the ancient world a large share of children never reached adulthood. Jews stood out among their neighbors for refusing to abandon unwanted newborns. Tacitus, who did not like Jews, recorded with distaste that they thought it a crime to kill any child born after the heir (Histories 5.5). Households that could afford it also held slaves, some of them fellow Jews sold for debt, and slaves fill Jesus's parables: trusted stewards, idle servants and debtors begging for time.

Sickness had few remedies. There were physicians, but they cost money and often failed; the woman with the flow of blood had spent everything she had on them (Mark 5:26). Some illnesses, such as the skin diseases of Leviticus 13, shut a person out from village life as well as from the Temple. Many assumed illness came from sin, which is why the disciples asked whose sin made a man blind (John 9:2). When Jesus healed, he gave people back their place among their neighbors as well as their health.

The dead were buried quickly, usually the same day. The body was washed and wrapped in linen with spices (John 19:40). Mourning was loud and public. The Mishnah, written down much later, says that even the poorest man in Israel should hire at least two flute players and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral (Ketubot 4:4), and Matthew 9:23 finds the flute players already at work in Jairus's house. Families who could afford it buried their dead in tombs cut into the rock, with niches for bodies. After about a year, when the flesh had gone, the bones were gathered into a carved stone box, an ossuary. Around Jerusalem this custom lasted roughly from 20 BC to AD 70 (L. Y. Rahmani's catalogue of ossuaries; Steven Fine). One ossuary, found in 1968 at Givat HaMivtar in Jerusalem, held the bones of a man named Yehohanan, with an iron nail about 11.5 centimeters long still driven through his heel bone. It is the only physical trace of a crucifixion yet found, and it shows that a crucified man could be given a family burial. Most tombs were closed with a square stone. The archaeologist Amos Kloner counted more than 900 burial caves from this period around Jerusalem and found only four with a round, rolling stone, all in the tombs of the very rich. Others, such as Urban von Wahlde, think the Gospel accounts still fit a smaller stone that could be rolled.

read.text: Because Joseph her husband was a righteous man and was unwilling to disgrace her publicly, he resolved to divorce her quietly.
read.note: Joseph and Mary were betrothed, which was as binding as marriage, so ending it meant divorce. The law and village honor were both on Joseph's side, and a public charge would have shamed Mary for life. Matthew calls his choice to protect her righteous.

read.text: It was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told this to the apostles. But their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women.
read.note: Josephus says a court would not take a woman's word. The apostles did not either. A writer inventing a story to persuade people in this world would not have made women its first witnesses, and Luke names them anyway.

read.text: So Joseph bought a linen cloth, took down the body of Jesus, wrapped it in the cloth, and placed it in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance to the tomb.
read.note: A rock-cut tomb was a rich family's grave, and Matthew calls Joseph of Arimathea a rich man (Matthew 27:57). If Kloner is right, a rolling stone was rarer still, the mark of a wealthy family's tomb. The body of a crucified man was laid where honored men were laid.

ancient.note: Written in the 70s AD by a Jewish general who fought Rome and then watched the siege from the Roman side. Cited here by book and section.

ancient.note: His defense of his own conduct, and his defense of the Jewish people and their law.
